lines.text: When a flood hits, twelve thousand people need food, water and medicine within thirty-six hours.
The shelters, the suppliers, the carriers and the registry that could help don't share a platform, so coordination still happens by phone and spreadsheet.
ReliefMesh changes that. It is five independent websites on the Open Agentic Web, each running its own agents on its own origin. Nobody has to adopt anyone's platform.
Press one button. Before any site is contacted, you're told which origin, why, and what will be sent. Nothing leaves the page until you say so.
The agents find the partners by URL and load their published networks from their own origins. Every request on this graph is real.
Each partner's attestation is verified right in your browser: the signature is checked, and the network file is hashed and compared with what the registry attested.
One supplier is unverified, priced far below the rest, and its notes tell the agent to approve immediately. It is flagged, excluded, and never obeyed.
A deterministic engine allocates every shortage within budget and explains each line. A model may explain the plan, but it cannot change a single number.
Nothing is written anywhere until a person approves. Then the reservation is confirmed in the supplier's own window, on the supplier's origin. Transport works the same way.
Shipments are tracked to delivery, and every consent, decision and receipt lands in a hash-chained audit trail.
Under the hood: the official runtime, unmodified. Twelve call paths passing the official partner check. Two hundred and sixty-seven automated tests. And an interoperability inspector anyone can use.
ReliefMesh. When disaster strikes, agents coordinate before humans have to.
